query: Single-phase high-entropy alloys have difficulty achieving a satisfactory strength–ductility balance. Earlier work introduced the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy with a uniform, fine lamellar structure to enable large-sized production and obtain good strength and plasticity, but its performance still falls short of industrial requirements. Its use in aircraft and spacecraft fasteners further requires stability under extreme temperature fluctuations, long-term mechanical loading, room-temperature creep, and corrosion, while relevant creep and corrosion studies remain limited by sample-size and experimental-environment constraints. Given these limitations and design requirements, what single intervention could improve the alloy’s practical performance? Present one hypothesis that specifies the intervention, causal mechanism, predicted improvement over the starting material, boundary conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a feasible experiment whose outcome could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a controlled microalloying addition of 1–2 atomic percent niobium (Nb) into the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy will improve its strength–ductility balance, creep resistance, and corrosion stability by forming stable, finely dispersed Nb-rich precipitates at the lamellar boundaries.
generation.material_initial_state: AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy with a uniform, fine lamellar microstructure.
generation.intervention: Addition of 1–2 atomic percent niobium (Nb) to the alloy composition.
generation.conditions: Performance evaluated under extreme temperature fluctuations, long-term mechanical loading (room-temperature creep), and corrosive environments.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of uniformly distributed, nanoscale Nb-rich precipitates along the lamellar interfaces.
generation.mechanism: The Nb-rich precipitates hinder dislocation motion and stabilize the microstructure, thereby enhancing strength, reducing creep deformation, and improving corrosion resistance through more robust interface passivation.
generation.predicted_outcome: The Nb-enhanced alloy will exhibit increased yield strength, improved creep resistance, and decreased corrosion rates compared to the baseline alloy while maintaining an acceptable level of ductility.
generation.baseline: Mechanical and corrosion performance metrics of the original AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy.
generation.boundary: These improvements are expected when Nb remains within the 1–2 atomic percent range and processing conditions are optimized to prevent precipitate coarsening; performance may be affected under conditions that destabilize the Nb-rich precipitates.
generation.uncertainty: The precise magnitude of performance enhancements and long-term microstructural stability under actual aerospace operating conditions remain to be confirmed.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of alloy samples: one set with the baseline AlCoCrFeNi2.1 composition and one set with 1–2 atomic percent Nb added. Process both sets under identical casting and heat-treatment conditions. Subject the samples to cyclic thermal loading to simulate extreme temperature fluctuations, long-term creep tests under constant load, and corrosion tests in a simulated corrosive environment.
measurements: Creep strain versus time under constant load
Corrosion rate and qualitative corrosion morphology
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Nb-enhanced alloy does not exhibit statistically significant improvements in yield strength, creep resistance, or corrosion performance compared to the baseline alloy (i.e., if any changes are within experimental error margins), the hypothesis is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: Adding a minor fraction of niobium (Nb) to the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy will promote the formation of stable, finely dispersed Nb-rich precipitates at the lamellar boundaries, leading to an improved balance of strength, ductility, creep resistance, and corrosion stability under extreme temperature fluctuations.
drafts.material_initial_state: AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy with a uniform, fine lamellar structure exhibiting good but insufficient strength and plasticity for aerospace fastener applications.
drafts.intervention: Introduce a controlled microalloying addition of approximately 1–2 atomic percent Nb to the alloy composition.
drafts.conditions: The Nb-enhanced alloy is processed under identical casting and heat-treatment conditions as the baseline material to control precipitate formation and avoid coarsening, and is evaluated under simulated extreme temperature fluctuations, long-term mechanical loading for room-temperature creep, and corrosive environments.
drafts.structural_mediator: Formation of uniformly distributed, nanoscale Nb-rich precipitates along the lamellar interfaces.
drafts.mechanism: These precipitates are expected to hinder dislocation motion and stabilize the microstructure against coarsening and grain-boundary degradation, thereby enhancing mechanical strength, improving creep resistance, maintaining ductility, and potentially offering more robust corrosion resistance through stabilization of interface regions.
drafts.predicted_outcome: The Nb microalloyed alloy will exhibit increased yield strength and creep resistance under prolonged mechanical loading, with minimal adverse effect on ductility, compared to the baseline alloy.
drafts.baseline: Performance metrics of the original AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic alloy, which meets some production and strength/ductility criteria but falls short under the extreme and long-term conditions required for aerospace fasteners.
drafts.boundary: This improvement is expected when the Nb addition remains within 1–2 atomic percent and when subsequent processing conditions prevent significant precipitate coarsening. The intervention may not be effective if the operating temperatures or corrosive conditions cause deleterious evolution of the Nb-rich precipitates.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of alloy samples: one set with the baseline AlCoCrFeNi2.1 composition and another set with a 1–2 at.% Nb addition. Process both sets under identical casting and heat-treatment conditions. Subject both sets to cyclic thermal loading (to mimic extreme temperature fluctuations), long-term room-temperature creep tests under constant load, and controlled corrosion tests in a relevant corrosive medium.
measurements: Creep strain vs. time under constant load
Corrosion rate and qualitative corrosion morphology analysis
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Nb-enhanced alloy does not demonstrate statistically significant improvements in yield strength, creep resistance, or corrosion performance relative to the baseline alloy (i.e., if changes fall within the measurement error margins), then the hypothesis that Nb microalloying improves practical performance is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: Introducing a small molybdenum addition (e.g., ~1–2 atomic%) into the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy will increase creep resistance and corrosion resistance without significantly degrading ductility or processability.
drafts.material_initial_state: As-cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy with a uniform, fine lamellar microstructure.
drafts.intervention: Partial substitution of Ni by approximately 1–2 at.% Mo during alloy melting or powder-based alloy synthesis.
drafts.conditions: Standard alloy casting or powder metallurgy routes, followed by the same post-processing (solution treatment and quenching) currently used to produce the baseline AlCoCrFeNi2.1 microstructure.
drafts.structural_mediator: Mo atoms will segregate to grain boundaries and/or form fine precipitates, modifying the lamellar microstructure and providing additional pinning against dislocation movement.
drafts.mechanism: The localized Mo-enrichment and/or Mo-based precipitates will hinder dislocation glide—leading to higher creep resistance at elevated temperatures—and increase pitting corrosion resistance, as Mo is known to enhance passivity in Fe-based alloys.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Compared to undoped AlCoCrFeNi2.1, the Mo-doped alloy should exhibit a measurable improvement in creep behavior at high temperature and superior corrosion resistance in chloride-containing environments, while retaining similar or slightly improved tensile strength and ductility.
drafts.baseline: Mechanical and corrosion properties reported for unmodified AlCoCrFeNi2.1 under the same thermal and loading conditions.
drafts.boundary: The positive effect of Mo additions may be most pronounced at moderate doping (1–2 at.%). Higher additions could produce detrimental brittle phases and reduce ductility, limiting the feasible compositional window.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize the baseline AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy and identical batches with 1 at.% and 2 at.% Mo added, employing the same casting and subsequent heat-treatment schedule.
measurements: High-temperature compression or tensile creep tests at an elevated temperature (e.g., 700–800°C) measuring time to failure or steady-state creep rate.
Potentiodynamic polarization tests in a 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution to quantify pitting corrosion resistance.
Room-temperature tensile tests to assess yield strength and ductility.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Mo-doped alloys show neither improved creep resistance nor enhanced corrosion performance compared to the baseline, or if they exhibit significantly reduced ductility, the hypothesis is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: Introducing a small addition of titanium (Ti) to the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy will enhance its creep resistance and corrosion resistance while maintaining its strength–ductility balance.
drafts.material_initial_state: AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy with a uniform, fine lamellar structure.
drafts.intervention: Add 1–2 atomic percent titanium (Ti) to the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy composition.
drafts.conditions: The alloy is subjected to extreme temperature fluctuations, long-term mechanical loading, room-temperature creep, and corrosive environments relevant to aerospace applications.
drafts.structural_mediator: Formation of Ti-rich precipitates and solid-solution strengthening effects.
drafts.mechanism: The addition of Ti is expected to promote the formation of fine, stable Ti-rich precipitates that act as obstacles to dislocation motion, thereby improving creep resistance. Ti also enhances passivation behavior in corrosive environments, improving corrosion resistance. These effects are achieved without significantly disrupting the fine lamellar structure, preserving the strength–ductility balance.
drafts.predicted_outcome: The modified alloy will exhibit improved creep resistance (e.g., lower steady-state creep rate by at least 20%) and enhanced corrosion resistance (e.g., lower corrosion current density by at least 15%) compared to the baseline AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy, while maintaining comparable strength and ductility.
drafts.baseline: The original AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy with its current strength–ductility balance, creep resistance, and corrosion resistance.
drafts.boundary: The hypothesis applies to Ti additions in the range of 1–2 atomic percent and under conditions relevant to aerospace applications, including extreme temperature fluctuations and corrosive environments.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloys with 1–2 atomic percent Ti additions and compare their creep resistance, corrosion resistance, and mechanical properties to the baseline alloy under simulated aerospace conditions.
measurements: Steady-state creep rate under long-term mechanical loading at elevated temperatures
Corrosion current density in a simulated corrosive environment
Tensile strength and ductility at room temperature
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Ti-modified alloy does not show at least a 20% improvement in creep resistance or a 15% improvement in corrosion resistance compared to the baseline, or if the strength–ductility balance is significantly degraded, the hypothesis will be falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: Introducing a controlled heat treatment process to the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy will enhance its strength and ductility balance by refining the microstructure and promoting phase stability.
drafts.material_initial_state: AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy with a uniform, fine lamellar structure.
drafts.conditions: Heat treatment at a specific temperature and duration to optimize microstructural characteristics.
drafts.structural_mediator: Refinement of grain size and enhancement of phase distribution.
drafts.mechanism: The heat treatment will promote the formation of a more stable microstructure, reducing defects and improving dislocation mobility, which in turn enhances both strength and ductility.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Improvement in the strength-ductility balance of the alloy, potentially achieving a yield strength increase of 10-20% while maintaining or improving ductility.
drafts.baseline: Current performance of AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy with limited strength and ductility under industrial conditions.
drafts.boundary: The hypothesis is valid within the temperature range of typical heat treatments and does not account for extreme environmental conditions outside of standard laboratory settings.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct a series of heat treatments on AlCoCrFeNi2.1 samples at varying temperatures and durations, followed by mechanical testing.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the heat-treated samples do not show a statistically significant improvement in both strength and ductility compared to untreated samples, the hypothesis will be falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: Introduction of a controlled amount of precipitate-forming elements to the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy can improve its strength-ductility balance and stability under extreme conditions.
drafts.material_initial_state: AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy with a uniform, fine lamellar structure
drafts.intervention: Addition of precipitate-forming elements (e.g., Ti, Nb) to the alloy composition
drafts.conditions: Extreme temperature fluctuations, long-term mechanical loading, room-temperature creep, and corrosion
drafts.structural_mediator: Precipitates formed by the added elements
drafts.predicted_outcome: Improved strength, ductility, and stability under extreme conditions
drafts.baseline: Current performance of the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy
drafts.boundary: Optimal amount and type of precipitate-forming elements, processing conditions, and service environment

falsification_experiment.design: Systematic variation of precipitate-forming element content and processing conditions, followed by mechanical testing and microstructural characterization
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the introduction of precipitate-forming elements does not result in a significant improvement in strength, ductility, and stability under extreme conditions, the hypothesis is falsified.
